meta.title: Build Your Own Trading Card Sorting Machine | Mault
meta.description: Step-by-step guide to building the Mault card sorter: bill of materials, wiring diagrams, 3D printed parts, firmware and assembly instructions.

hero.title: Build the card sorter
hero.modulesIntro: Each module has an IR sensor and three servos: a <0>bottom</0> paddle that acts as its floor, a side <1>paddle</1> gate and a left/right <2>pusher</2>. A card falls through every open bottom paddle until it lands on a closed one, then that module's pusher sweeps it into the left or right bin. With every bottom open it drops into the catch-all.

setup.heading: Set up your build
setup.description: Choose how you're building the sorter. The parts list, wiring and assembly steps below follow these choices, which are saved in this browser.

kit.title: A Mault kit
kit.description: ESP32-S3 on its breakout board, 3 modules, and the firmware already flashed. Bring your own 6V 3A power supply.

diy.title: Sourcing my own
diy.description: Buy the parts from the list below and pick your own board and module count.

board.label: Controller board

uno_r4.description: 5V logic. Connects to the app over USB.

esp32.description: 3.3V logic. Connects to the app over USB or Bluetooth.

board.kitLocked: Set by the kit. Choose "Sourcing my own" to change it.

raspberry-pi.description: 40-pin GPIO header · Linux host and controller

orange-pi-zero4.description: GPIO header · Linux host and controller

breakout.title: On a breakout board
breakout.description: The ESP32 plugs into a breakout board. Uses Plate 14 "ESP 32 Breakout": the ESP32 breakout mount plate and a tall base fitted with the base panel esp.

bare.title: Bare board
bare.description: Wire straight to the ESP32's pins. Uses the ESP32 mount plate from Plate 16.

modules.label: Sorting modules
modules.description: Each module adds two bins. With the catch-all at the bottom, that's {{bins}} bins.

setup.shopNote: Would rather not source every part yourself? The <0>Mault shop</0> sells kits with everything except the 3D-printed parts. You'll still need to print those yourself.

bom.heading: Bill of materials
bom.description: Quantities follow your module count: {{modules}} modules × 3 servos plus 1 feeder servo, and {{irSensors}} IR sensors. That uses {{channelsUsed}} of the PCA9685's 16 channels, and one PCA9685 runs up to 5 modules. Check off each part as you gather it. Checkmarks are saved in this browser.
bom.affiliateDisclaimer: Some "Buy" links are Amazon affiliate links. We may earn a small commission on qualifying purchases at no extra cost to you.
bom.kitPowerSupplyNote: Kits don't include a power supply. You'll need your own regulated 6V supply rated for at least 3A to power the servos.
bom.kitCollapsedNote: You're building from a kit, so the parts list is collapsed. Open it if you want to check any part.

unoR4.notes: Runs {{path}}; USB connection to the host computer for Web Serial

esp32.notes: Runs {{path}}; USB connection to the host computer for Web Serial. Once it's set up, the app can also flash it directly.

esp32WithBreakout.part: ESP32-S3-WROOM-1 N16R8 board with GPIO screw-terminal expansion adapter
esp32WithBreakout.notes: Runs {{path}}; USB connection to the host computer for Web Serial. The board plugs into the adapter for screw-terminal wiring. Sold as a 2-pack, so you get a spare.

pca9685.notes: I²C servo driver, drives every servo in the sorter

sg90Positional.partSpec: (0.09 s/60° at 4.8 V, 8 µs dead zone)
sg90Positional.notes: 3 per module × {{count}} modules: bottom paddle, side paddle gate, pusher
sg90Positional.alert: Avoid Tower Pro SG90s. They don't hold their calibrated positions reliably in this sorter.

mg90sContinuous.notes: Feeder, drives cards out of the hopper into module 1

irSensor.notes: One at the gate of each module (1-{{count}}), plus one in the hopper throat

psu.notes: Dedicated servo power into the PCA9685 V+ terminal. Never power the servos from the {{board}}'s onboard 5V. 5.5mm x 2.5mm barrel plug, center positive.

usbCableEsp32.notes: ESP32-S3 dev board ↔ host computer. Plug it into the board's left USB-C port (labeled USB), not the right one (labeled UART or COM).

barrelJack.part: DC barrel jack or screw-terminal pigtail
barrelJack.notes: Adapts the PSU output to the PCA9685's V+ / GND terminal

filament.notes: Quantity per your slicer's estimate for the model above

oRing.notes: Fitted onto the feeder roller for grip on the card face

hopperORing.notes: Fits onto the hopper idler roller

servoControllerPlate.notes: Printed once, regardless of module count

binsPlate.notes: card bin large, card bin medium and card bin small. Catch the cards the pusher ejects to each side

endBinPlate.notes: end card tray. Used alongside the Bins to complete the bin assembly

m3x6Screw.notes: 14 attach each bin base to the housing; 8 attach the base panels to the base; 2 mount a camera or phone bracket

m3Nut.notes: Paired with the base panel M3×6 screws

m3Washer.notes: Included in the M3 screw kit. Used with the M3×8 screws that mount the hopper idler roller

m3x25Screw.notes: Adjusts the hopper idler roller tension with the spring

hopperSpring.notes: Tensions the adjustable wall against the card stack

m2x6Screw.partSpec: (17 per module, +4 for the board mount, +3 for the servo driver board, +1 for the feeder)
m2x6Screw.notes: Per module: the paddle and pusher arms, plus 6 to fix the bottom and side paddles to the housing. The rest mount the {{board}}, the PCA9685 and the feeder.

m2x8Screw.notes: 2 per module ({{count}} modules), to mount the pusher. M2×10 works fine if you don't have M2×8 on hand.

servoHornScrew.notes: Secures each horn to its servo shaft

hookupWire.notes: For the IR sensors and servos. If one is too short, join two and wrap the joint in electrical tape so it can't pull apart.

wagoConnectors.notes: Splices power and ground to each IR sensor without twisting/soldering wires together

dupontConnectors.notes: These are only needed if you're making your own custom length wires.

webcam.notes: This is the one I use. Any webcam works as long as you can manually adjust focus, brightness, etc. (auto-adjusting can throw off scans)

ankerC200.notes: Recommended alternative to the C920. Also lets you manually adjust focus, brightness, etc.

cameraMountScrew.notes: Standard tripod-mount thread, screws into a webcam or phone mount's socket

hopperWeights.notes: Drop into the weighted hopper sled to press the stack down so cards feed more reliably. Add up to 25

m10Washer.notes: Optional extra weight for the hopper weight

servoExtensionCables.notes: Only needed for more than 3 sorting modules, where the stock servo leads won't reach the servo driver board

feederBearings.notes: For the bearing feeder base (Plate 4 "Alternative Feeder Base"), so the roller spins more smoothly

neodymiumMagnets.notes: Disc magnets, 5 mm across and 2 mm thick

wiring.description: Everything hangs off one I²C bus (PCA9685) and {{count}} digital input pins (IR sensors). The {{board}}'s onboard supply powers the PCA9685's logic side. Its <pin>V+</pin> servo rail must come from the external supply, and that supply's ground must be tied back to the {{board}}'s ground.
wiring.wireColorNote: Wire colors vary between parts and suppliers, so don't rely on the colors in the diagram or photos. Trace each wire from its pin label and make sure it ends up at the correct place.
wiring.powerSupplyWarning: Use a 6V 3A power supply for the servos. Anything higher can burn out the servos or the servo control board.

i2c.title: I²C bus
i2c.esp32Note: Wire PCA9685 VCC to the ESP32's 3.3V pin, not 5V. The I²C pull-ups follow whatever powers the PCA9685, and feeding 5V into an ESP32 GPIO can damage it. The PCA9685 chip itself runs its logic fine at 3.3V, so this costs nothing.

diagram.title: Wiring diagram
diagram.alt: Wiring diagram showing the PCA9685, microcontroller, servo, and IR sensor connections
diagram.anyColorNote: The wire colors in the diagram are only there to make it easier to read. Your wires can be any color, as long as each one connects the right pins.

irSensors.description: All {{count}} read active-LOW (pin goes low when a card is present) using the {{board}}'s internal pull-up. Wire the sensor's digital OUT straight to the pin, no external pull-up resistor needed.
irSensors.esp32Note: Power these sensors' VCC from the ESP32's 3.3V pin if the module supports it, not 5V. Their digital OUT tends to swing up to whatever VCC they're fed, and 5V on OUT risks damaging the GPIO it's wired to. Check your specific sensor's datasheet accepts 3.3V.

channelMap.unused: Unused, available for additional sorting modules

assembly.heading: Assembly
assembly.description: Work through the phases in order, structural work first. Checkboxes are saved in this browser, so you can close the tab mid-build and pick back up later.
assembly.helpText: Stuck on a step? Join the Discord if you need help.

printSortingModule.text: Print Plate 1 "Sorting Module - Print to Need" {{count}} times, once per sorting module, from the <mesh>MakerWorld model</mesh> (or re-export from <source>Card Sorter.f3d</source>). Each print is one complete module: sorting module base, card platform, bottom paddle, left paddle, right paddle, card pusher left, card pusher right, bottom paddle linkage, left paddle linkage, right paddle linkage, 2 pusher linkage, bottom paddle servo horn, side paddles servo horn (no spline) and pusher servo horn.
printSortingModule.alternativesNote: Optional: Plate 2 "Alternative Horns" has loose fit and snug fit versions of every servo horn, for servos whose shafts fit the standard horns too tightly or too loosely.

printFeederModule.text: Print Plate 3 "Feeder Module" once, regardless of module count: feeder base (flat), roller, roller servo horn (MG90S), hopper, hopper idler roller (small), hopper adjustable wall (side-print version) and feeder ramp (steep). The feeder ramp is required for reliable feeding, so print it even though it's a separate piece.
printFeederModule.alternativesNote: If roller servo horn (MG90S) fits your feeder servo too tightly or too loosely, print roller servo horn, roller servo horn (loose fit) or roller servo horn (snug fit) from Plate 2 "Alternative Horns" instead. Using the optional ball bearings? Print Plate 4 "Alternative Feeder Base" (feeder base (flat, bearing version) and feed roller (bearing version)) in place of the feeder base and roller.

printSortingModuleShroud.text: Print Plate 5 "Sorting Module Shroud" once: the camera shroud that sits over the stacked modules, plus the phone mount and two camera mounts. You only need the mount for the camera you use.

printPlateBase.text: For {{modules}} sorting modules, print {{threeTall}} tall bases (3 units high) and {{oneTall}} short bases (1 unit high) from Plate 6 "Base Support - Print to Need". The tall base is base frame module (tall, open) with its 2 base panels, and the short base is base frame module. Each print has one of each, so print only the pieces you still need. The modules stack in a staircase, so each added tier needs one more unit of height than the tier above it. Mix the two heights to build up each tier.
printPlateBase.breakoutText: For {{modules}} sorting modules, print {{threeTall}} tall bases (3 units high) and {{oneTall}} short bases (1 unit high) from Plate 6 "Base Support - Print to Need". The tall base is base frame module (tall, open) with its 2 base panels, and the short base is base frame module. Each print has one of each, so print only the pieces you still need. Plate 14 "ESP 32 Breakout" counts as one more tall base: its base frame module (tall, open) takes one base panel and the base panel esp, which leaves room for the breakout board. The modules stack in a staircase, so each added tier needs one more unit of height than the tier above it. Mix the two heights to build up each tier.
printPlateBase.alternativeNote: Optional: Plate 18 "Alternative Panel" has base panel finger hole to swap in for either base panel.

printPlateBaseBottom.esp32OrArduino: Print your board plate from Plate 16 "Circuit Boards": Arduino mount plate (with standoffs) for an Arduino Uno R4, or ESP32 mount plate (with slots) for a bare ESP32 board. Print only the one for your board.
printPlateBaseBottom.esp32Breakout: Print Plate 14 "ESP 32 Breakout" once instead of a Plate 16 board plate. Its ESP32 breakout mount plate holds the ESP32 on its breakout board, and the same print has the panelled tall base and 10 module alignment pins.

printServoControllerPlate.text: Print Plate 7 "Servo Controller Plates" once: servo controller mount plate, plus folding wing left and folding wing right.

printEndBottom.text: Print Plate 8 "End Plate" once: end mount plate, plus folding wing left, folding wing right and folding wing end.

printGenericBase.text: For {{modules}} sorting modules, print Plate 9 "Generic Plate - Print to Need" {{count}} times. Each print is one blank mount plate with a folding wing left and folding wing right.
printGenericBase.alternativeNote: Optional: Plate 13 "Optional - Regular Bin Holders" has fixed wings (bin wing left, bin wing right and bin wing end) to use instead of the folding wings on Plates 7, 8 and 9.

printBinsPlate.text: Print Plate 10 "Bins" twice. Each print has 3 bins: card bin large, card bin medium and card bin small. Plate 20 "Additional Bins" has a card bin XL if you need a bigger bin.
printBinsPlate.risersNote: If you're using more than 3 modules, you may need the module riser from Plate 15 "Bin Riser" to raise the back two bins high enough.

printEndBinPlate.text: Print Plate 11 "End Bin" once: end card tray.

printModulePins.text: Print {{count}} module alignment pin pieces for {{modules}} sorting modules: {{top}} for the tops and {{front}} for the fronts of the base pieces. Plate 6 "Base Support - Print to Need" has 16 per print (Plate 14 has 10 more), so print just the pins from it until you have enough. Each base piece takes 4 pins on top, and each unit of height takes 2 on the front, except the top unit of each column. The pins join the base pieces together and hold the sorting modules on the base.
printModulePins.glueAlert: Glue the pins into the supports. Dry-fit the base pieces and sorting modules with the pins first, then once everything lines up, super glue each module alignment pin into place.

dryFit.text: Dry-fit each module housing before inserting any electronics. Sand or adjust any tight servo pockets now.

printOptionalPlates.text: Optional: Plate 12 "Optional Facades" has the frame front plate and three frame back plates (frame back plate, frame back plate (feeder) and frame back plate (Arduino)). Plate 17 "Hopper Weights" has card weight v2 and card weight (small) to press the stack down, and Plate 19 "Hopper Accessories" has the hopper extension for a taller stack.

flashInBrowser.text: Easiest option: install the firmware straight from this browser.
flashInBrowser.unsupported: (Needs a Chromium-based browser such as Chrome or Edge.)
flashInBrowser.note: Plug the ESP32-S3 into your computer by its left USB-C port (labeled USB) first. Works on a brand new ESP32-S3. If the flash succeeds, skip the rest of this phase: the steps below are the manual Arduino IDE route.

downloadCode.text: Download the code from the <repo>GitHub repository</repo> (Code → Download ZIP) and unzip it, then open the firmware folder with the Arduino IDE (File → Open → firmware/main/main.ino).
downloadCode.note: The Arduino IDE needs a sketch to live in a folder with the same name, so open main.ino from inside firmware/main rather than moving it elsewhere.

installEsp32Core.text: In the Arduino IDE, add the ESP32 board index URL (File → Preferences → Additional boards manager URLs): https://raw.githubusercontent.com/espressif/arduino-esp32/gh-pages/package_esp32_index.json, then install "esp32 by Espressif Systems" from the Boards Manager.
installEsp32Core.note: This pulls down a few hundred MB (the whole Xtensa toolchain) and takes a few minutes.

installLibraries.text: In the Arduino IDE, install the ArduinoJson, Adafruit PWM Servo Driver, and Adafruit NeoPixel libraries.

installLibrariesEsp32.note: Library Manager → search each by name. Bluetooth support ships with the ESP32 core you just installed, so no extra Bluetooth library is needed.

installLibrariesUnoR4.text: In the Arduino IDE, install the ArduinoJson, Adafruit PWM Servo Driver, Adafruit NeoPixel, and ArduinoBLE libraries.
installLibrariesUnoR4.note: Library Manager → search each by name. ArduinoBLE powers Bluetooth on the Uno R4 WiFi. The Uno R4 Minima has no Bluetooth hardware and doesn't use it, so Minima builds can skip it.

uploadSketch.text: Select board "Arduino UNO R4 WiFi" (or "Arduino UNO R4 Minima" if that's the one you have), select the correct port, then upload firmware/main/main.ino.
uploadSketch.note: Picking the exact board matters: Bluetooth is only compiled in when the WiFi board is selected.

uploadSketchEsp32.text: Plug the board into your computer using its left USB-C port (labeled USB, not UART). Select board "ESP32S3 Dev Module", set Tools → USB Mode to "Hardware CDC and JTAG" and USB CDC On Boot to "Enabled", select the correct port, then upload firmware/main/main.ino.
uploadSketchEsp32.note: Both USB settings are required: without them the board doesn't show up on its native USB port, and the in-app browser flasher can't reliably reset it into bootloader mode without a BOOT-button press. The tradeoff is that the board enumerates under a generic Espressif name instead of "Mault Card Sorter". The sketch already has the ESP32-S3 pin layout (see the IR_PINS comment in main.ino).

confirmReady.text: Open the Serial Monitor at 9600 baud and confirm you see {"status":"ready"} after the board resets.

intro.horns: Leave every horn off its servo shaft in this phase. You fit the paddles and pusher arms to their horns now, but the horns only go onto the servos in the app's setup wizard (Wire and calibrate), once each servo has moved to the right position.
intro.linkages: The linkages are labeled LEFT and RIGHT, matching the left and right of the platform.

mountModuleServos.text: Install the bottom, paddle and pusher servos, all 180° positional SG90s, into each of the {{modules}} module housings (sorting module base from Plate 1): {{count}} servos in total.

mountBottomFlapper.text: Assemble the bottom paddle from the Plate 1 pieces: screw bottom paddle to bottom paddle linkage, then the linkage to bottom paddle servo horn. Screw the assembled bottom paddle into the module housing with 2 M2×6 screws.
mountBottomFlapper.note: This paddle is the module's floor. It opens to drop a card to the next module.

mountSideFlappers.text: Assemble the side paddles from the Plate 1 pieces: screw left paddle to left paddle linkage and right paddle to right paddle linkage, then both linkages to side paddles servo horn (one set per module). Screw the assembled side paddles into the module housing with 4 M2×6 screws.
mountSideFlappers.note: One servo drives both side paddles, so they open and close as a pair.

mountPusherArm.text: Assemble the pusher from the Plate 1 pieces: screw card pusher left and card pusher right to the two pusher linkage pieces, then both linkages to pusher servo horn. Screw the assembled pusher into the module housing with two M2×8 screws.

fitFeederOrings.text: Fit the 6 feeder O-rings (20 mm ID) onto the roller from Plate 3.
fitFeederOrings.note: These give the roller grip on the card face. Space them evenly along the roller's length.

mountRollerHorn.text: Press roller servo horn (MG90S) (Plate 3) onto the shaft of the continuous-rotation feeder servo and secure it with the horn screw.
mountRollerHorn.note: The horn is the small piece that fits the servo shaft. Neither roller part has "servo" printed on it.

mountFeederServo.text: Pass the horn, now on the servo, through the hole in feeder base (flat), then slide the roller onto the horn. The horn seats inside the roller so the servo turns it.

fitHopperRollerOrings.text: Fit the 4 hopper O-rings (9.2 mm ID) onto the hopper idler roller (small) (Plate 3).
fitHopperRollerOrings.note: Same as the feeder roller, these give it grip on the card face.

mountHopperRoller.text: Install the hopper idler roller (small) into place on the hopper (both Plate 3) with 2 M3×8 screws and 2 M3 washers.
mountHopperRoller.note: The roller should be stiff once mounted. It should not free-roll.

calibrateHopperRoller.text: Fit the spring and M3×25 screw, then tighten the screw until it pokes out from the bottom of the mounting point. Slowly back it off until the hopper feeds only 1 card at a time.

mountHopperRiser.text: Install the feeder ramp (steep) (Plate 3) on the back of the hopper.
mountHopperRiser.requiredAlert: Required: don't skip the feeder ramp. The feeder doesn't feed cards reliably without it.

mountModuleIr.text: Fix one IR sensor at the gate of each module (1-{{modules}}) with 1 M2×6 screw each, aimed across the card path.

mountHopperIr.text: Fix the remaining IR sensor in the hopper throat, just above the feeder, with 1 M2×6 screw.
mountHopperIr.note: This one tells the feeder when the hopper is empty. Placement matters more than the module sensors.

wireI2c.text: Wire the PCA9685 to the {{board}}'s I²C bus (SDA/SCL) and logic power/GND.
wireI2c.bendPinsNote: The PCA9685's header pins point straight out to the side. You may need to bend them 90° upward so they clear the panel and stay easy to reach when wiring to the {{board}}.

wireServos.text: Wire all {{count}} servos into PCA9685 channels 0–{{lastChannel}} and 15 per the channel map. The feeder always takes the last channel.
wireServos.note: Wire channels in the side of the base, with zip-tie points, keep the cables tidy.

wireSensors.text: Wire the {{count}} IR sensors to the digital pins in the table below. Module gates and the hopper throat sensor don't all fall on consecutive pins.
wireSensors.note: The sensors share power and ground: join the {{count}} power wires into one and the {{count}} ground wires into one, using Wago connectors, a breadboard or solder. You'll set each sensor's range in a later step.

wirePower.text: Bring the external 6V supply into the PCA9685 V+/GND terminal, and tie its ground to the {{board}}'s ground.
wirePower.note: Skipping the common ground is the #1 cause of servos that twitch but never move correctly.

connectSerial.text: Connect the {{board}} to the app via Web Serial, then open /app/calibrate.

connectSerialEsp32.text: Plug the {{board}} into your computer using its left USB-C port (labeled USB, not UART), connect it to the app via Web Serial, then open /app/calibrate.

calibrateModules.text: Module by module, set the open and closed positions of the bottom paddle and the side paddles, and the left, neutral and right positions of the pusher.
calibrateModules.note: For the pusher's left and right positions, swing the arm toward the inner wall but stop before it touches, about 15-16% away from neutral. The pusher doesn't need to hit the wall to fling the card, and pressing against it strains the servo. The app warns you past 16%.

installHorns.text: In the setup wizard (Set up your sorter), install the horns one servo at a time, each with its paddle or pusher arm already fitted. Bottom paddle and side paddles: move the slider to 90%, then press the horn onto the servo shaft with the paddle in its closed position. Pusher: move the slider to 50%, then press the horn onto the shaft. Secure each horn with its horn screw, for all {{count}} module servos.
installHorns.note: The wizard opens the first time the sorter connects, and any time from the help (?) menu on /app/calibrate. A horn fitted off-center biases the whole linkage. The exact positions get fine-tuned in the next step.

calibrateFeeder.text: In the Feeder panel, tune feed speed, pulse/pause timing and settle duration against your actual hopper.

adjustIr.text: Set all {{count}} IR sensors to see a card 1 inch (2.5 cm) in front of them. With the board powered, use a small screwdriver on the screw of each sensor's blue box (the potentiometer). First turn it until the sensor's indicator LED goes off with nothing in front of it. Then hold a card 1 inch in front of the sensor and turn the screw slowly back the other way until the LED just comes on.
adjustIr.note: Check it by pulling the card back to about 2 inches (5 cm): the LED should go off again. If it stays on, back the screw off a little. A sensor set too far reaches past the card path and reports cards that aren't there.

checkIr.text: In the IR Sensors panel, hold a card in front of each of the {{count}} sensors and confirm it reports the card, then clears when you take the card away.
checkIr.note: If a sensor doesn't trigger, or triggers with nothing in front of it, repeat the previous step for that sensor.

testBins.text: With Bin Routing, send a test card to each of the {{count}} bins in turn and confirm it lands correctly.

loadHopper.text: Load the hopper and confirm the feeder stops pulsing once the hopper IR reads empty.

fullPass.text: Run a full scan-to-bin pass end to end before leaving the unit unattended.

printModel.description: Every printed part of a {{count}}-module sorter, colored by what to print. The key lists how many of each you need, numbered by plate in the print file. Change the module count or board in the setup above and the model and counts update.
printModel.label: 3D model of a {{count}}-module card sorter, colored by printed part
printModel.hint: Drag to rotate, scroll to zoom, right-drag to pan. Hover or tap a part in the key to show only that part.

pi.logic: Use a PCA9685 board that supports 3.3V logic power and signals. Connect VCC to physical pin 1 (3.3V), never 5V. Pi SDA, SCL and GPIO inputs must not receive 5V. Disconnect all power before wiring.
pi.sensors: IR sensor OUT must be 3.3V safe. Power compatible sensors from 3.3V, or use a suitable level shifter for 5V outputs. Connect sensor grounds to Pi GND. Numbers in this table are physical header pins, not GPIO line numbers.
pi.power: Power the Pi with its own model-appropriate supply. Plug the separate 6V servo supply into the barrel adapter and connect the adapter’s + and − leads to PCA9685 V+ and GND. Keep the Pi-to-PCA9685 logic GND connection. Never connect servo 6V to Pi power or logic VCC.
pi.connect: Open your own Mault installation and select the built-in GPIO sorter. The Pi controls the sorter directly; no USB serial connection is needed.
pi.install: Install Mault on this Pi using the Pi/Linux GPIO installation guide before calibrating.
pi.mount: Mount the Pi securely with insulated standoffs or a suitable case. The Arduino/ESP32 printed controller plate does not fit these boards.
pi.essentials: Pi power supply, boot storage, GPIO jumper wires and USB camera
pi.requirements: Use a supported Linux installation, storage and power supply appropriate for your Pi model, GPIO jumper wires, and a supported USB camera. Raspberry Pi models need the 40-pin GPIO header. The Pi hosts Mault and controls the sorter directly.
pi.diagramAlt: {{board}} wiring diagram with physical header pins, 3.3V logic and separate servo power.
pi.boardNotes: The Pi hosts Mault and controls the sorter directly. Raspberry Pi models require the 40-pin GPIO header.
pi.overview: Use one I²C bus for the PCA9685 and {{count}} digital inputs for the IR sensors. The {{board}} supplies the PCA9685 logic power and connects to its logic GND. The separate servo power supply plugs into the barrel adapter; the adapter’s positive and negative leads connect to PCA9685 <pin>V+</pin> and <pin>GND</pin>. The servo supply does not come from the Pi.
pi.wirePower: Connect the separate 6V servo power supply through the barrel adapter to PCA9685 V+ and GND.
